collection.description: A villager could tell it as the old ones always did, solemn and slow, with a moment of silence for each person lost.

ask.text:
On the last night of the year, the village sits up together until dawn, and the eldest tells the story of the year: every birth, every loss, every storm and every good catch. This year (name) is the eldest, and (he/she) has been thinking for weeks about how to tell it.
(Name) could tell it as the old ones always did, solemn and slow, with a moment of silence for each person lost. Or (he/she) could tell it the way (he/she) would want to hear it, with the funny parts too.
How should (name) tell the story of the year?

c1o1.text: There are tears for the people lost, and quiet nods for the hard days. But by the time the sky turns grey, everyone feels lighter, as if the year has been put down gently somewhere safe. They watch the first sunrise of the new year together, and nobody speaks, and nobody needs to.

c1o2.text: (Name) tells it beautifully, and when dawn comes (he/she) is exhausted, and looks it. The long night has settled into (his/her) face. (He/She) looks every one of (his/her) years now, and somehow more like an eldest than ever. "Worth it," (he/she) says, and goes to sleep for most of the first day of the year.

c1.text: (Name) tells it slowly, solemnly, by the firelight, every name and every day, and the village sits in silence, listening...

c2o1.text: The tears and the laughter come together, which is the way the year really was. By dawn, everyone is red-eyed and aching from laughing, and they watch the sunrise leaning on each other. "Next year," someone says, "it'd better be a funny one too."

c2o2.text: Telling the funny parts, (name) laughs harder than (he/she) has in years, and something about the long night of laughing seems to wash the years out of (his/her) face. By dawn (he/she) looks years younger, and swears (he/she) feels it too. "Laughing," (he/she) says, "is the best medicine the healers never thought of."

c2.text: (Name) tells the hard parts gently, and then tells about the fish that jumped into the wrong canoe, and the night the pigs got into the stores, and the village starts to laugh...
